contenido: 1. THE DIGNITY OF WOMEN and their vocation, a constant object of human and Christian reflection, has assumed a very particular importance in recent years. This is demonstrated, among other things, by the interventions of the Magisterium of the Church, reflected in several documents of the Second Vatican Council, which in the Final Message states: «The time has come, the time has come when the vocation of women is fully fulfilled, the time when women acquire in the world an influence, a weight, a power never achieved until now. Therefore, at this moment in which humanity is experiencing such a profound mutation, women filled with the spirit of the Gospel can help so much that humanity does not decline. secular.(3)

2. The last Synod took place during the Marian Year, which offers a particular impetus to address this issue, as also indicated by the Encyclical Redemptoris Mater.(9) This Encyclical develops and updates the teaching of the Second Vatican Council contained in chapter VIII of the dogmatic Constitution Lumen gentium on the Church. This chapter has a significant title: "The Holy Virgin Mary, Mother of God, in the Mystery of Christ and the Church." Mary – this “woman” of the Bible (cf. Gén 3, 15; Jn 2, 4; 19, 26) – belongs intimately to the saving mystery of Christ and for this reason she is also present in a special way in the mystery of the Church. Since "the Church is in Christ like a sacrament (...) of the intimate union with God and the unity of the entire human race", (10) the special presence of the Mother of God in the Mystery of the Church makes us think of the exceptional bond between this "woman" and the entire human family. Here we are talking about each and every one of the sons and daughters of the human race, in whom, in the course of generations, that fundamental inheritance of all humanity is realized, united with the mystery of the biblical principle: "So God created the human being in his own image, in the image of God he created him, male and female he created them" (Gén 1, 27).(11)

3. "When the fullness of time arrived, God sent his Son, born of a woman." With these words from the Letter to the Galatians (4, 4) the apostle Paul relates among themselves the main moments that essentially determine the fulfillment of the mystery "pre-established in God" (cf. Ef 1,9). The Son, the Word consubstantial with the Father, is born as a man from a woman when "the fullness of time" arrives. This event takes us to the key point in the history of man on earth, understood as the history of salvation. It is significant that the Apostle does not call the Mother of Christ by the proper name of "Mary", but rather calls her "woman", which establishes an agreement with the words of the Protoevangelium in the Book of Genesis (cf. 3, 15). Precisely that "woman" is present in the central salvific event, which decides the "fullness of time" and which is realized in her and through her.

4. In this way "the fullness of time" manifests the extraordinary dignity of "woman." This dignity consists, on the one hand, in the supernatural elevation to union with God in Jesus Christ, which determines the profound purpose of each man's existence both on earth and in eternity. From this point of view, "woman" is the representative and archetype of the entire human race, that is, she represents that humanity that is characteristic of all human beings, whether men or women. On the other hand, the event of Nazareth highlights a way of union with the living God, which is typical only of the "woman", of Mary, that is, the union between mother and son. In effect, the Virgin of Nazareth becomes the Mother of God.

5. This event has a clear interpersonal character: it is a dialogue. We do not fully understand it if we do not place the entire conversation between the angel and Mary in the greeting: "full of grace." (19) The entire dialogue of the annunciation reveals the essential dimension of the event: the supernatural dimension (***). But grace never dispenses with nature or annuls it, but rather perfects and ennobles it. Therefore, that "fullness of grace" granted to the Virgin of Nazareth, in anticipation of her becoming "Theotókos", means at the same time the fullness of the perfection of what "is characteristic of woman", of "what is feminine". We find ourselves here, in a certain sense, at the climax, the archetype of the personal dignity of women.

6. We must place ourselves in the context of that biblical "principle" according to which the truth revealed about man as the "image and likeness of God" constitutes the immutable basis of all Christian anthropology. (22) "So God created the human being in his own image, in the image of God he created him, male and female he created them" (Gén 1, 27). This concise fragment contains the fundamental anthropological truths: man is the apex of everything created in the visible world, and the human race, which has its origin in the call to existence of man and woman, crowns all the work of creation; both are human beings to the same degree, both man and woman; both were created in the image of God. This image and likeness to God, essential to the human being, is transmitted to their descendants by men and women, as husbands and parents: "Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth and subdue it" (Gén 1, 28). The Creator entrusts the "domain" of the earth to the human race, to all people, both men and women, who receive their dignity and vocation from that common "principle."

7. Penetrating with thought the entire description of the Book of Genesis 2, 18-25, and interpreting it in the light of the truth about the image and likeness of God (cf. Gén 1, 26-27), we can better understand what the personal character of the human being consists of, thanks to which both "man and woman" are similar to God. In fact, each man is the image of God as a rational and free creature, capable of knowing and loving him. We further read that man cannot exist "alone" (cf. Gén 2, 18); it can exist only as a "unity of the two" and, therefore, in relation to another human person. It is a reciprocal relationship, of man with woman and woman with man. Being a person in the image and likeness of God also involves existing in relation to the other "I." This is a prelude to the definitive self-revelation of God, One and Triune: living unity in the communion of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.

8. The presentation of man as "the image and likeness of God", as it appears immediately at the beginning of the Holy Scripture, also has another meaning. This fact constitutes the key to understanding biblical Revelation as a manifestation of God about himself. Speaking of himself, whether "through the prophets, or through the Son" made man (cf. Heb 1, 1-2), God speaks a human language, uses human concepts and images. If this way of expressing itself is characterized by a certain anthropomorphism, its reason lies in the fact that man is "like" God, that is, created in his image and likeness. Consequently, God is also, to a certain extent, "like" man and, precisely on the basis of this similarity, he can become known by men. At the same time, the language of the Bible is precise enough to show the limits of "similarity," the limits of "analogy." Indeed, biblical revelation affirms that while the "likeness" of man with God is true, the "non-likeness" that distinguishes all creation from the Creator is even more essentially true. In short, for man created in the likeness of God, God himself is the one "who dwells in an inaccessible light" (1 Tim 6, 16): He is the "Diverse" by essence, the "totally Other."

9. "Constituted by God in a state of holiness, man, tempted by the Evil One, from the beginning of history abused his freedom, setting himself up against God and longing to achieve his end outside of God."(28) With these words the teaching of the last council evokes the revealed doctrine on sin and, in particular, on that first sin, which is the "original." The biblical "beginning" - the creation of the world and of man in the world - contains within itself at the same time the truth about this sin, which can also be called the sin of the "beginning" of man on earth. Although the Book of Genesis' account of this event is expressed symbolically, as in the description of the creation of man as male and female (cf. Gén 2, 15-25), it nevertheless reveals what must be called "the mystery of sin" and, more properly still, "the mystery of evil" in the world created by God.

10. The biblical description of the Book of Genesis outlines the truth about the consequences of man's sin, as well as indicating the alteration of that original relationship between man and woman, which corresponds to the personal dignity of each of them. Man, both male and female, is a person and, therefore, "the only creature on earth that God has loved for itself"; and at the same time precisely this unique and unrepeatable creature "cannot find its own plenitude if not in the sincere gift of itself to others." (32) From here arises the relationship of "communion", in which the "unity of the two" and the dignity as a person of both man and woman are expressed. Therefore, when we read in the biblical description the words addressed to the woman: "Your desire will go towards your husband and he will dominate you" (Gén 3, 16), we discover a rupture and a constant threat precisely in relation to this "unity of the two", which corresponds to the dignity of the image and likeness of God in both. But this threat is more serious for women. Indeed, by being a sincere gift and, consequently, by living "for" the other, dominance appears: "he will dominate you." This "dominance" indicates the alteration and loss of the stability of that fundamental equality, which in the "unity of the two" man and woman possess; and this, above all, to the disadvantage of women, while only equality, resulting from the dignity of both as persons, can give the reciprocal relationship the character of an authentic "communio personarum." If the violation of this equality, which is jointly a gift and right that derives from God the Creator himself, entails an element of disadvantage for women, at the same time it also diminishes the true dignity of man. We touch here on an extremely delicate point in the dimension of that "ethos", originally inscribed by the Creator in the very fact of the creation of both in his image and likeness.

11. The Book of Genesis bears witness to the sin that is the evil of the "beginning" of man, as well as its consequences that since then weigh on the entire human race, and at the same time contains the first announcement of the victory over evil, over sin. This is proven by the words we read in Genesis 3:15, generally called "Protoevangelium": "I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring: he will tread on your head while you lie in wait for his heel." It is significant that the announcement of the redeemer, the savior of the world, contained in these words, refers to "the woman", who is named in the Protoevangelium in the first place, as the progenitor of the one who will be the redeemer of man. "father of lies" (Jn 8, 44) is the first author of sin in the history of man, this will also be the enmity between him and woman.

12. The words of the Protoevangelium in the Book of Genesis allow us to move to the realm of the Gospel. The redemption of man announced there becomes a reality here in the person and mission of Jesus Christ, in whom we also recognize what the reality of redemption means for the dignity and vocation of women. This meaning is clarified by the words of Christ and by the set of his attitudes towards women, which is extremely simple and, precisely for this reason, extraordinary if one considers the environment of his time; It is an attitude characterized by extraordinary transparency and depth. Various women appear in the course of the mission of Jesus of Nazareth, and the encounter with each of them is a confirmation of the evangelical "newness of life", which has already been spoken of.

13. Going through the pages of the Gospel, a large number of women, of different ages and conditions, pass before our eyes. We find women suffering from illnesses or physical suffering, like that woman possessed by “a spirit that made her sick; she was bent over and could not in any way straighten herself" (Lc 13, 11), or like Simon's mother-in-law who was "in bed with the fever" (Mc 1, 30), or like the woman "who suffered from an issue of blood" (cf. Mc 5, 25-34) and who could not touch anyone because she thought that her touch made the man "impure." All of them were healed, and the last one, the hemorrhagic woman, who touched Jesus' cloak "among the people" (Mc 5, 27), deserved the Lord's praise for her great faith: "Your faith has saved you" (Mc 5, 34). We also find Jairus' daughter whom Jesus brought back to life tenderly saying: "Girl, I tell you, get up" (Mc 5, 41). On another occasion it is the widow of Naim to whom Jesus brings her only son back to life, accompanying his gesture with an expression of affectionate pity: «He had compassion on her and said to her: "Do not cry"» (Lc 7, 13). Finally we see the Canaanite woman, a figure who deserved from Christ some words of special appreciation for her faith, her humility and for that greatness of spirit of which only the heart of a mother is capable: «Woman, great is your faith; May it happen to you as you wish" (Mt 15, 28). The Canaanite woman begged for her daughter's healing.

14. Jesus enters the historical and concrete situation of the woman, who carries the inheritance of sin. This inheritance is manifested in those customs that discriminate against women in favor of men, and is also rooted in her. From this point of view the episode of the woman "caught in adultery" (cf. Jn 8, 3-11) appears particularly eloquent. Jesus, at the end, tells her: "Sin no more," but first he makes the men who accuse her aware of their sin in order to stone her, thus manifesting his profound ability to see, according to the truth, human consciences and works. Jesus seems to say to the accusers: is this woman with all her sin perhaps not also, and above all, confirmation of your transgressions, of your "masculine" injustice, of your abuses?

15. The way of acting of Christ, the Gospel of his works and his words, is a coherent reproach to everything that offends the dignity of women. For this reason, women who find themselves with Christ discover themselves in the truth that he "teaches" and that he "performs," ​​even when this is the truth about their own "sinfulness." Through this truth they feel "liberated", reintegrated into their own being; They feel loved by an "eternal love", by a love that finds the most direct expression in Christ himself. Being under the radius of action of Christ, his social position is transformed; They feel that Jesus is talking to them about issues that in those times it was not customary to discuss with a woman. An example, in some ways very significant in this regard, is that of the Samaritan woman at the well of Shechem. Jesus – who in fact knows that she is a sinner and speaks to her about it – dialogues with her about the deepest mysteries of God. It speaks to him of the infinite gift of God's love, which is like "a fountain springing up to eternal life" (Jn 4, 14); He speaks to him about God who is Spirit and about true worship, which the Father has the right to receive in spirit and truth (cf. Jn 4, 24); He finally reveals to him that He is the Messiah promised to Israel (cf. Jn 4, 26).

16. From the beginning of Christ's mission, women demonstrate towards him and towards his mystery a special sensitivity, which corresponds to a characteristic of her femininity. It must also be said that this finds a particular confirmation in relation to the paschal mystery; not only at the moment of crucifixion but also on the day of resurrection. The women are the first to arrive at the tomb. They are the first to find it empty. They are the first to hear: "He is not here, he has risen as he had announced" (Mt 28, 6). They are the first to hug his feet (cf. Mt 28, 9). They are also the first to be called to announce this truth to the apostles (cf. Mt 28, 1-10; Lc 24, 8-11). The Gospel of John (cf. también Mc 16, 9) highlights the special role of Mary of Magdala. She is the first to find the resurrected Christ. At first he mistakes him for the garden's guardian; She recognizes him only when he calls her by name: «Jesus says to her: "Mary." She turns and says to him in Hebrew: "Rabbuni" âwhich means: "Teacher"â. Jesus said to him: "Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to the Father. But go to my brothers and tell them: I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God." Mary Magdalene went and told the disciples that she had seen the Lord and that he had spoken these words” (Jn 20, 16-18).

17. Let us now make virginity and motherhood the object of our meditation, as two particular dimensions of the realization of the feminine personality. In the light of the Gospel these acquire the fullness of their meaning and value in Mary, who as Virgin becomes Mother of the Son of God. These two dimensions of the feminine vocation have met and united in her in an exceptional way, so that one has not excluded the other, but has admirably completed it. The description of the Annunciation in the Gospel of Saint Luke clearly indicates that this seemed impossible to the Virgin of Nazareth herself. She, upon hearing that they say to her: "You are going to conceive in the womb and you are going to give birth to a Son whom you will call the name Jesus," then asks: "How can this be, since I do not know a man?" (Lc 1, 31. 34). In the common order of things, motherhood is the result of the reciprocal "knowledge" of man and woman in the marital union. Mary, firm in the purpose of her virginity, asks the divine messenger and obtains the explanation: "The Holy Spirit will come upon you", your motherhood will not be a consequence of a marital "knowledge", but the work of the Holy Spirit, and "the power of the Most High" will extend its "shadow" over the mystery of the conception and birth of the Son. As the Son of the Most High, he is given to you exclusively by God, in the way known to God. Mary, therefore, has maintained her virginal “I know no man” (cf. Lc 1, 34) and at the same time has become a mother. Virginity and motherhood coexist in her, without mutually excluding each other or setting limits; Furthermore, the person of the Mother of God helps everyone – especially women – to glimpse the way in which these two dimensions and these two paths of the vocation of the woman, as a person, explain and complete each other.

18. To take part in this “glimpse,” it is necessary once again to delve deeper into the truth about the human person, as presented by the Second Vatican Council. Man – male or female – is the only terrestrial creature that God has loved for himself, that is, he is a person, he is a subject who decides about himself. At the same time, man "cannot find his own plenitude if it is not in the sincere gift of himself to others." (39) It has already been said that this description - which in a certain sense is the definition of the person - corresponds to the fundamental biblical truth about the creation of man - man and woman - in the image and likeness of God. This is not a purely theoretical interpretation or an abstract definition, since it essentially indicates the meaning of being a man, highlighting the value of the gift of self, of the person. This vision of the person also contains the essential part of that “ethos” that “referring to the truth of creation” will be fully developed by the Books of Revelation and, in a particular way, by the Gospels.

19. We return in our reflection to the biblical paradigm of "woman" taken from the Protoevangelium. The "woman", as mother and as the first educator of man (la educación es la dimensión espiritual del ser padres), has a specific precedence over man. If her motherhood, considered above all in a biophysical sense, depends on man, she prints an essential "sign" on the entire process of making the new sons and daughters of the human race grow as people. A woman's motherhood, in a biophysical sense, manifests an apparent passivity: the process of formation of a new life "takes place" in her, in her organism, deeply involving it. At the same time, motherhood from the personal-ethical aspect expresses a very important creativity of women, on which the very humanity of the new creature depends decisively. Also in this sense, women's motherhood represents a special call and challenge addressed to men and their fatherhood.

contenido: 20. In the teachings of Christ, motherhood is linked to virginity, although they are different things. For this purpose, Jesus' phrase said in the colloquium on the indissolubility of marriage is fundamental. Upon hearing the answer that the Lord gave to the Pharisees, the disciples said to him: "If such is the condition of a man with respect to his wife, there is no point in marrying" (Mt 19, 10). Regardless of the meaning that "it doesn't matter" then had in the minds of the disciples, Christ takes advantage of the occasion of that erroneous opinion to instruct them about the value of celibacy; distinguishes celibacy due to natural defects – including those caused by man – from “celibacy for the Kingdom of heaven.” Christ says: “There are eunuchs who made themselves such for the Kingdom of heaven” (Mt 19, 12). Consequently, it is a free celibacy, chosen by the Kingdom of heaven, in consideration of man's eschatological vocation to union with God. And he adds: "Whoever can understand, let him understand." These words are a reiteration of what he had said when he began to talk about celibacy (cf. Mt 19, 11). Therefore, this celibacy for the Kingdom of heaven is not only the result of a free choice on the part of man, but also of a special grace on the part of God, who calls a determined person to live celibacy. If this is a special sign of the Kingdom of God that is to come, at the same time it serves to dedicate all the energies of the soul and body to this eschatological Kingdom in an exclusive way, during temporal life.

21. Virginity in the evangelical sense involves the renunciation of marriage and, therefore, also of physical motherhood. However, the renunciation of this type of motherhood, which can even entail a great sacrifice for the woman's heart, opens up the experience of motherhood in a different sense: motherhood "according to the spirit" (cf. Rom 8, 4). Indeed, virginity does not deprive a woman of her prerogatives. Spiritual motherhood takes many forms. In the life of consecrated women who, for example, live according to the charisma and rules of the different Institutes of an apostolic nature, this motherhood can be expressed as concern for men, especially for those most in need: the sick, the handicapped, the abandoned, the orphans, the elderly, children, the young, the imprisoned and, in general, the marginalized. A consecrated woman finds the Husband in this way, different and unique in each and every one, according to his own words: "As you did it to one of these... you did it to me" (Mt 25, 40). Spousal love always entails a singular availability to pour itself into all who are within the radius of its action. In marriage, this availability – even though it is open to everyone – consists in a particular way in the love that parents give to their children. In virginity this availability is open to all men, embraced by the love of Christ the Bridegroom.

22. The Gospel reveals and allows us to understand precisely this way of being of the human person. The Gospel helps each woman and each man to live it and, in this way, to fulfill themselves. There is, in fact, a total equality regarding the gifts of the Holy Spirit and the "wonders of God" (Act 2, 11). And not only this. Precisely in the face of the "wonders of God" the man-Apostle feels the need to resort to what is essentially feminine, to express the truth about his own apostolic service. This is how Paul of Tarsus expresses himself when he addresses the Galatians with these words: "My children, for whom I am again in labor pains" (Gál 4, 19). In the first Letter to the Corinthians (7, 38) the apostle announces the superiority of virginity over marriage – a constant doctrine of the Church according to the words of Christ, as we read in the Gospel of Saint Matthew (19, 10-12) – but without in any way obfuscating the importance of physical and spiritual motherhood. In fact, to illustrate the fundamental mission of the Church, the Apostle cannot find anything better than the reference to motherhood.

23. The words of the Letter to the Ephesians are of fundamental importance in relation to this topic: “Husbands, love your wives as Christ loved the Church and gave himself up for her, to sanctify her, cleansing her by the bath of water, by virtue of the word, and to present her resplendent to himself; without spot or wrinkle or any such thing, but be holy and spotless. This is how husbands should love their wives as their own bodies. He who loves his wife loves himself. For no one ever hated his own flesh; rather, he feeds it and cares for it with affection, just as Christ does the Church, since we are members of his Body. Therefore a man will leave his father and mother and be united to his wife, and the two will become one flesh. This is a great mystery, I say it with respect to Christ and the Church” (5, 25-32).

24. The text addresses husbands, as concrete women and men, and reminds them of the "ethos" of spousal love that goes back to the divine institution of marriage from the "beginning." The exhortation "husbands, love your wives" responds to the truth of this institution, love them as a requirement of that special and unique union, through which man and woman become "one flesh" in marriage (Gén 2, 24; Ef 5, 31). In this love there is a fundamental affirmation of the woman as a person, an affirmation thanks to which the feminine personality can be fully developed and enriched. This is how Christ acts as the husband of the Church, desiring her to be “resplendent, without spot or wrinkle” (Ef 5, 27). It can be said that everything that constitutes "the style" of Christ in treating women is fully reflected here. The husband would have to make the elements of this style his own with his wife; and, in an analogous way, a man should do so, in any situation, with a woman. In this way both, woman and man, realize the "sincere gift of themselves."

25. In the text of the Letter to the Ephesians we find a second dimension of the analogy that as a whole must serve to reveal "the great mystery." This is a symbolic dimension. If the love of God towards man, towards the chosen people, Israel, is presented by the prophets as the love of the husband for the wife, such an analogy expresses the "spousal" condition and the divine and non-human character of God's love: "Your husband is your Maker (...), God of the whole earth is called" (Is 54, 5). The same can be said of the spousal love of Christ the Redeemer: "For God so loved the world that he gave his only Son" (Jn 3, 16). It is, therefore, the love of God expressed through the redemption accomplished by Christ. According to the Pauline letter, this love is "similar" to the spousal love of spouses but naturally it is not "equal." Analogy, in effect, implies a similarity, but leaves an adequate margin of non-similarity.

26. In the vast background of the "great mystery", which is expressed in the spousal relationship between Christ and the Church, it is also possible to adequately understand the fact of the call of the "Twelve." Christ, calling only men as his apostles, did so in a totally free and sovereign way. And she did so with the same freedom with which in all her behavior she highlighted the dignity and vocation of women, without conforming to the dominant usage and tradition supported by the legislation of her time. Therefore, the hypothesis that he called some men as apostles, following the mentality widespread in his time, does not completely reflect Christ's way of acting. «Teacher, we know that you are truthful and that you teach the way of God with frankness..., because you do not look at the condition of people» (Mt 22, 16). These words fully characterize the behavior of Jesus of Nazareth; in this we also find an explanation for the call of the "Twelve." All of them were with Christ during the Last Supper and only they received the sacramental command: "Do this in memory of me" (Lc 22, 19; 1 Cor 11, 24), which is linked to the institution of the Eucharist. They, on the afternoon of the day of the resurrection, received the Holy Spirit to forgive sins: «Whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven; from whom you retain, they remain retained” (Jn 20, 23).

27. The Second Vatican Council has renewed awareness in the Church of the universality of the priesthood. In the New Covenant there is only one sacrifice and only one priest: Christ. All the baptized participate in this one priesthood, whether men or women, in that they must "offer themselves as a living victim, holy and pleasing to God" (cf. Rom 12, 1), bear witness to Christ in every place and give a reason for their hope in eternal life to whoever asks (cf. 1 Ped 3, 15).(51) Universal participation in the sacrifice of Christ, with which the Redeemer has offered the entire world to the Father and, in particular, humanity, makes everyone in the Church constitute "a kingdom of priests" (Ap 5, 10; cf. 1 Ped 2, 9), that is, they participate not only in the priestly mission, but also in the prophetic and royal mission of Christ the Messiah. This participation also determines the organic union of the Church, as the People of God, with Christ. With it the "great mystery" of the Letter to the Ephesians is expressed at the same time: the Bride united to her Husband; united, because she lives her life; united, because it participates in its triple mission («tria munera Christi»); united in such a way that she responds with a "sincere gift" of herself to the ineffable gift of love of the Bridegroom, Redeemer of the world. This concerns everyone in the Church, both women and men, and obviously also concerns those who participate in the "ministerial priesthood",(52) which has the character of service. Within the scope of the “great mystery” of Christ and the Church everyone is called to respond “like a bride” with the gift of life to the ineffable gift of the love of Christ, who, as Redeemer of the world, is the only Bridegroom of the Church. In the “royal priesthood,” which is universal, the gift of the Bride is expressed at the same time.

28. "The Church believes that Christ, who died and was resurrected for all, gives man his light and his strength through the Holy Spirit, so that he can respond to his highest vocation."(56) We can apply these words from the Council Constitution Gaudium et spes to the topic of this reflection. The particular call to the dignity of women and their vocation, typical of the times in which we live, can and must be welcomed with the "light and strength" that the Spirit generously gives to man, also to the man of our time, so rich in multiple transformations. The Church "believes that the key, the center and the end" of man, as well as "of all human history, is found in its Lord and Master" and affirms that "beneath the surface of change there are many permanent things, which have their ultimate foundation in Christ, who exists yesterday, today and forever." (57)

29. The previously cited text from the Letter to the Ephesians (5, 21-33), where the relationship between Christ and the Church is presented as the bond between the Husband and the Wife, also refers to the institution of marriage according to the words of the Book of Genesis (cf. 2, 24). The same text unites the truth about marriage, as a primordial sacrament, with the creation of man and woman in the image and likeness of God (cf. Gén 1, 27; 5, 1). With the significant comparison contained in the Letter to the Ephesians, it becomes completely clear what determines the dignity of women both in the eyes of God – Creator and Redeemer – and in the eyes of man, male and female. On the foundation of God's eternal plan, woman is the one in whom the order of love in the created world of people finds a ground for its first root. The order of love belongs to the intimate life of God himself, to the Trinitarian life. In the intimate life of God, the Holy Spirit is the personal hypostasis of love. Through the Spirit, the uncreated Gift, love becomes a gift for created people. Love, which comes from God, is communicated to creatures: "The love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us" (Rom 5, 5).

30. The dignity of a woman is closely related to the love she receives for her femininity and also to the love that, in turn, she gives. This confirms the truth about the person and about love. Regarding the truth of the person, we must turn once again to the Second Vatican Council: "Man, the only terrestrial creature whom God has loved for himself, cannot find his own plenitude except in the sincere gift of himself to others."(59) This refers to every man, as a person created in the image of God, whether man or woman. The ontological nature statement contained here also indicates the ethical dimension of the person's vocation. A woman cannot find herself if she does not give love to others.

31. “If you knew the gift of God” (Jn 4, 10), Jesus says to the Samaritan woman during one of those admirable conversations that show the great esteem that Christ has for the dignity of women and for the vocation that allows them to take part in his messianic mission.
